title: V. Managing Human Resources in the Public Sector

segments.text: Public-sector HRM covers recruitment, careers, performance, development, and fair treatment specifically within government employment — shaped by law, merit principles, political accountability, and formal service rules in ways the general HRM material in the Business Administration chapter does not need to address. blocks.text: .4 Closed versus Open Systems of Public Employment

The trade-off, worth stating precisely: closed systems build institutional memory, continuity, and a strong shared professional identity, at some cost to bringing in fresh specialist expertise or introducing external competitive pressure; open systems can inject specialized skills and competitive dynamism more readily, at some cost to long-term institutional continuity and the depth of internal career-based commitment.

The general HRM function set (workforce planning, recruitment, selection, training, performance management, rewards, employee relations, succession planning) applies to government organizations largely as covered in the Business Administration chapter’s HRM unit — the distinctive public-sector overlay is that each of these functions typically operates under specific statutory service rules and constitutional protections (security of tenure, structured appeal rights against disciplinary action) that private-sector HRM does not need to observe in the same form.

items.text: The three foundational contrasts — spoils vs. merit, personnel management vs. HRM, closed vs. open systems — each describe a genuine trade-off, not a simple “correct” and “incorrect” side; a strong answer states both sides’ strengths and limitations.

Public-sector HRM functions mirror the general HRM cycle from the Business Administration chapter, but operate inside statutory service rules and constitutional protections that shape (and sometimes constrain) how each function can actually be applied.
